paper_title: MEND: RL For Flow Models via Proximal Velocity Matching

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Reward post-training of flow models either reweights the model's own samples under a KL penalty or a frozen reference, often for thousands of updates, or backpropagates the reward and moves every sample without checking that the move is worth its size. We introduce MEND, a reinforcement learning method built on proximal velocity matching. MEND caps rewards within each prompt group, so samples that already score well receive no move. Below the cap, it proposes moves along the reward gradient and accepts one only when its capped reward gain exceeds a quadratic displacement price. The model then regresses onto the resulting velocity targets, with no KL term, frozen reference model, or advantage weights. In 100 updates, MEND outperforms Flow-GRPO (about 4k updates) on five of six evaluators at the same distance to base-model images. Under an equal-budget protocol, it surpasses ReFL and DiffusionNFT at every evaluated update across four training rewards, reaching PickScore 24.03 versus 23.92 and 23.43, respectively. A 300-update three-reward run also surpasses the five-reward DiffusionNFT model on all three rewards it trains on. MEND is general and easy to adopt: it applies to any flow backbone with a differentiable reward.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Learned reward models make it possible to post-train text-to-image flow models for human preference (Kirstain et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2023). The open problem is how to turn scalar score into an update that raises reward quickly without eroding what the base model already does well. score alone does not say which samples should change or where they should go. Policy-gradient methods such as Flow-GRPO reweight stochastic trajectories by group-relative advantages under KL penalty (Liu et al., 2025). Weighted-regression methods such as DiffusionNFT reweight the models own samples inside regression loss (Zheng et al., 2026). Both adjust how much existing samples count, and the Flow-GRPO and DiffusionNFT models we compare against use about 4k and 1.7k updates. Reward backpropagation supplies direction: ReFL and DRaFT differentiate the reward through sampling (Xu et al., 2023; Clark et al., 2024). But the gradient moves every sample, including those that already score well, and nothing checks that move earns its size. KL penalty or reference term limits drift of the distribution as whole and makes no per-sample decision. The three-mode example of Figure 2 shows both failures: reweighting suppresses hard mode, and unchecked ascent pushes samples into low-density regions. Table 1: Objective components. Blue matches MEND; red differs. The check compares reward gain with displacement cost. MEND uses lagged behavior adapter, not frozen reference. Updates refer to the compared runs. Method Flow-GRPO ReFL DiffusionNFT MEND KL / frozen reference Reward weights Target check Updates yes no yes no yes no yes no no yes no yes no no no yes 4k 100 1.7k 100 We introduce MEND, an RL method for flow models based on proximal velocity matching (Figure 4). Its principle is that sample should move only when the reward it gains pays for the distance it travels. Within each prompt group, MEND caps rewards at quantile, so samples that already score well keep their place. For each sample below the cap, it proposes few moves along the normalized reward gradient and selects the candidate with the highest capped reward minus quadratic displacement price, with the unchanged sample always among the candidates. This is proximal-point step evaluated on decoded candidates. The model then regresses its velocity at stored rollout state onto the behavior velocity shifted by the accepted displacement, with no KL term, frozen reference model, or advantage weights  (Table 1)  . The selection rule comes with guarantees. Every accepted target improves capped reward by more than its quadratic price, and its displacement bound shrinks to zero as the sample approaches the cap (Proposition 1). At the behavior parameters, the descent direction of the regression loss backpropagates normalized reward gradients through the clean predictions of accepted samples only, scaled by their selected steps (Proposition 2).

After 100 PickScore updates, MEND outperforms Flow-GRPO, trained for about 4k updates, on every evaluator except aesthetic score, at the same distance to base-model images  (Table 2)  . Under the equal-budget protocol of Zhou et al. (2026), it surpasses ReFL and DiffusionNFT at every evaluated update on all four training rewards (Figures 1 and 8). Figures 1 and 3 show matched visual comparisons. Our contributions are: Insight and method. We observe that existing reward post-training never decides, sample by sample, whether change is worth making. We propose MEND, which makes this decision explicit through proximal velocity matching: sample receives new velocity target only when its capped reward gain exceeds quadratic displacement price, and the model is trained by plain regression onto these targets, with no KL term, frozen reference model, or advantage weights. Theory. We prove that every accepted target improves reward by more than its displacement price, with displacement bound that vanishes as the sample approaches the cap (Proposition 1). We further show that the resulting regression gradient is reward backpropagation restricted to the accepted samples and scaled by their selected steps (Proposition 2). Performance and generality. In only 100 updates, MEND outperforms Flow-GRPO (about 4k updates) on five of six evaluators at the same base distance. At equal budget, it surpasses ReFL and DiffusionNFT on all four training rewards, reaching PickScore 24.03 versus 23.92 and 23.43. MEND is backbone-agnostic and easy to adopt: the same method improves SD3.5-M, SD3-M and the distilled Z-Image-Turbo at the same update budget.

sections.title: 4.1 SETUP
sections.content: We train SD3.5-M (Esser et al., 2024) on PickScore under the equal-budget protocol of Zhou et al. (2026): 48 Pick-a-Pic prompts (Kirstain et al., 2023) 24 images per update, rank-32 LoRA, 10-step rollouts at 512 pixels, and 100 updates. ReFL and DiffusionNFT are the baselines under this protocol. We also compare with the Flow-GRPO PickScore adapter (Liu et al., 2025) (about 4k updates) and the five-reward DiffusionNFT model (Zheng et al., 2026) (1.7k updates). Evaluation uses DrawBench (Saharia et al., 2022), 200 prompts 5 seeds and 40 Euler steps, scored with PickScore, HPSv2.1 (Wu et al., 2023), HPSv3 (Ma et al., 2025), ImageReward (Xu et al., 2023), CLIPScore (Hessel et al., 2021) and aesthetic quality (Schuhmann et al., 2022). Fidelity is the DreamSim distance (Fu et al., 2023) to the base image generated with the same prompt, noise and sampling settings. Appendix B.1 gives baseline settings, and Appendix D.1 repeats the main comparison on DrawBench prompts held out from all design decisions.

sections.title: 4.2 MAIN COMPARISON
sections.content: MEND outperforms Flow-GRPO on five of six evaluators at the same base distance (0.313), with roughly 40-fold fewer updates  (Table 2)  . Aesthetic score is the one evaluator on which Flow-GRPO is higher (5.90 versus 5.88). The run trained on PickScore, HPSv2.1 and CLIPScore surpasses DiffusionNFT (1.7k updates on five rewards) on those three evaluators at smaller base distance, and is lower on HPSv3, ImageReward and aesthetic score, which it does not train on. Table 2 and Figures 5 to 7, except Figure 6(a), use each models headline sampling setting; Table 3 and Figures 1 and 8 use the equal-budget protocols setting (Appendix B). Section 4.3 compares equal budgets. Figure 5 shows DrawBench examples where MEND renders counts, attributes or spatial relations that SD3.5-M misses from the same noise.

sections.title: 4.3 UPDATE EFFICIENCY AND FIDELITY
sections.content: At equal budget, MEND is ahead of both baselines at every evaluated update. In Figure 1(b), it reaches PickScore 24.03 at update 100, versus 23.92 for ReFL and 23.43 for DiffusionNFT. On 64 unseen Pick-a-Pic prompts (Figure 6(a)), it is above DiffusionNFT under the same protocol at every evaluated update. By update 25 it also surpasses the levels of Flow-GRPO and DiffusionNFT, which use about 4k and 1.7k updates, respectively. Training costs 10.0 GPU-hours on 3 GB200 GPUs, excluding evaluation, and the result is stable across launches: second launch of the same configuration differs by 0.01 PickScore at update 50 (Appendix F.2). Reward keeps improving while base distance barely changes late in training: between updates 25 and 100, DrawBench PickScore rises from 23.36 to 23.70, while base distance moves only from 0.294 to 0.313 (Table 2, Figure 6(c)). Figure 7 follows two seeds through this run.

sections.title: 4.5 ABLATIONS
sections.content: The cap and the price decide which samples receive move, and together they preserve diversity: against moving every seed below the cap, the full rule keeps 0.037 more diversity for 0.35 PickScore  (Table 12)  . We vary one component at the development budget (16 prompts 8 images per update, 50 updates, the earlier optimizer setting). Table 12 in Appendix evaluates the checkpoints on full DrawBench; Figure 9 uses the development split, where the fixed-step control is available. MEND accepts target moves for 34% of seeds per round, reaching PickScore 23.10 at diversity 0.297. Removing the cap or the price raises this share to 45% and 78%, respectively, and lowers diversity to 0.287 and 0.291. Assigning move to every seed below the cap (81%) yields the highest full-set PickScore, 23.45, and lowest diversity, 0.260. At the full per-update budget, varying the initial price, using one candidate or removing the behavior EMA changes update-50 PickScore by at most 0.06; five candidates lower it by 0.25 (Appendix F.2).

sections.title: 4.6 QUALITATIVE RESULTS
sections.content: In matched comparisons, MEND corrects prompt errors of the base while keeping its composition. Figures 1, 3, 5, 7, 10 and 11 use matched prompts and initial noise, with PickScore on each tile. Figures 3 and 11 compare MEND with Flow-GRPO and DiffusionNFT; Figure 10 shows baseto-MEND pairs. sections.title: 5 RELATED WORK
sections.content: DDPO and DPOK optimize rewards with policy gradients, while Diffusion-DPO fits offline preferences (Black et al., 2024; Fan et al., 2023; Wallace et al., 2024). Flow-GRPO and DanceGRPO extend group-relative policy gradients to flow models with stochastic sampling and KL penalty (Liu et al., 2025; Xue et al., 2025). DiffusionNFT, AWM and FlowAWR use rewardor advantage-weighted regression on modelgenerated samples (Zheng et al., 2026; Xue et al., 2026; Fu et al., 2026). These methods adjust the contribution of existing samples; MEND instead constructs new local targets and verifies each one (Appendix H). ReFL, DRaFT and AlignProp backpropagate differentiable rewards through sampling (Xu et al., 2023; Clark et al., 2024; Prabhudesai et al., 2023); RAFT and related methods select among existing samples (Dong et al., 2023; Lee et al., 2026). Concurrently, Zhou et al. (2026) regress clean predictions toward bounded reward-gradient targets using group weights, while Self-OPD distills the models own stochastic branches (Zhang et al., 2026). MEND accepts proposal only when its capped reward gain over the unchanged sample exceeds quadratic displacement penalty. This per-target check differs from distribution-level Wasserstein regularization (Fan et al., 2025; Hwang et al., 2026). Figure 11: Matched comparisons with FlowGRPO and DiffusionNFT. Same prompt and seed per row; PickScore on each tile, best in bold.

sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION
sections.content: MEND post-trains flow models by proximal velocity matching: samples target moves only when its capped reward gain exceeds quadratic displacement price, and the model regresses onto the resulting velocity targets. This one per-sample rule replaces KL penalties, frozen reference models and advantage weights. In 100 updates, MEND outperforms Flow-GRPO on every evaluator except aesthetic score at the same distance to base-model images, and it surpasses ReFL and DiffusionNFT at equal budget on four rewards. MEND is backbone-agnostic and easy to adopt: it improves SD3.5-M, SD3-M and the distilled Z-Image-Turbo at the same update budget. At 10.0 GPU-hours for the SD3.5-M run, reward post-training becomes cheap enough to repeat for each new reward or backbone. Limitations. MEND requires differentiable reward. Its guarantees hold for the targets of each round. Longer training can over-optimize reward, and some single-reward runs lose held-out score within the 100-update budget (Appendices E.3 and F.4).

sections.title: H EXTENDED RELATED WORK
sections.content: Flow-GRPO, DanceGRPO, DiffusionNFT and AWM (Liu et al., 2025; Xue et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2026; Xue et al., 2026) reweight the models own samples and, with KL penalty of weight β, target the tilt πβ π eR/β; ReFL, DRaFT and AlignProp (Xu et al., 2023; Clark et al., 2024; Prabhudesai et al., 2023) move every sample along by an amount set by the learning rate. Few of these papers report diversity: FDFO (McAllister et al., 2026), ReNFT (Bao et al., 2026) and Adjoint Matching (Domingo-Enrich et al., 2025) use DreamSim, and ORW-CFM-W2 (Fan et al., 2025) and DMDR (Jiang et al., 2026a) use CLIP-embedding and LPIPS distances. Selection methods keep the best of samples (Dong et al., 2023), fit samples found by test-time search (Lee et al., 2026), accept or reject at an intermediate noise level (Anil et al., 2026) or rank fresh candidates (Jiang et al., 2026b); inference-time guidance (Bansal et al., 2024; Chung et al., 2023; He et al., 2024; Meng et al., 2022) applies the reward gradient to the sampler instead of to training targets.
